subject: Copywriting
title: Burger King: Where's Herb?
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Burger King: Where's Herb?.

hook.text: In 1985, Burger King spent $40 million on 'Where's Herb?'—a man who'd never eaten a Whopper. Nobody cared who Herb was.

buildup.text: The campaign asked customers to spot Herb in restaurants for prizes. It was a mystery game tied to the brand.

discovery.text: The problem: the concept emphasized NOT eating at Burger King. Herb's inexperience was the joke.

twist.text: When Herb was finally revealed on live TV, it was anticlimactic. $40 million for a man in glasses nobody remembered.

climax.text: AdAge called it 'the most elaborate advertising flop' of the 1980s. The slogan died, and so did the CMO's career.

punchline.text: $40 million wasted. Never make your brand the punchline.

quiz.question: Why did Burger King's 'Where's Herb?' campaign fail?
options: The concept emphasized not eating at Burger King

details.summary: In 1985 Burger King launched the 'Where's Herb?' campaign, spending $40 million to find a fictional character who had never eaten a Whopper. The campaign confused customers, failed to drive sales, and is remembered as one of advertising's greatest disasters — a cautionary tale about slogans that...
details.whyItMatters: Where's Herb shows what happens when cleverness replaces clarity. Studying famous failures teaches as much about slogan craft as studying successes.
takeaways: The $40 million campaign confused audiences about its purpose
Mystery-driven slogans fail when the payoff is underwhelming
Clarity of message should always precede creative ambition

faq.question: Why did the 'Where's Herb?' campaign fail?
faq.answer: Customers didn't understand who Herb was or why they should care. The campaign relied on mystery without emotional stakes. When Herb was finally revealed as a nerdy actor, the payoff felt pointless and the campaign collapsed.

faq.question: What lesson does 'Where's Herb?' teach about slogan writing?
faq.answer: A slogan must communicate clear value even if it uses intrigue or mystery. If people don't understand what you're selling or why it matters, no amount of spending will save the campaign. Clarity is not the enemy of creativity.
